title: Redundancy in Software Systems
description: What redundancy means in engineering, when to add spare capacity vs duplication, and how it improves reliability without wasting cost.
author: Pawan Bisht

blocks.text: Redundancy is having more than one way to perform a critical function so that a single failure does not take the whole system down. Search engines love clear definitions — this article explains redundancy for builders, not buzzwords.

blocks.title: In one line
blocks.text: Redundancy trades cost and complexity for the ability to survive partial failures.

items: Deployments introduce bugs — rolling back needs healthy instances.
Traffic spikes need headroom, not perfect sizing.

columns.title: Active / active
columns.body: All nodes serve traffic. Load balancers spread work. Fast failover but needs careful data consistency.

columns.title: Active / passive
columns.body: Standby waits until health checks fail. Cheaper, but failover time depends on detection + promotion.

columns.title: N+1 capacity
columns.body: Run N nodes worth of load on N+1 machines. One failure still leaves enough capacity for peak.

entries.definition: Recovery Time Objective — how long you can be down.
Recovery Point Objective — how much data loss is acceptable.
How much of the system one failure can affect.

items.text: Health checks on every redundant tier

items.title: Is redundancy the same as backup?
items.body: Backups recover past data; redundancy keeps live service available during failure. You usually want both.

items.title: When is redundancy overkill?
items.body: For low-criticality internal tools with tolerant users, a single region and good backups may be enough.
